core.text: 2 Related Work
2.1 Adversarial Risks in Human-AI Interaction

Most adversarial AI research targets the model itself through accuracy degradation, data manipulation, or information extraction [88, 27]. A smaller but growing body of work examines how such attacks influence human decision-making. Model-level studies show that perturbations to predictions can indirectly alter human reliance, and that the timing and context of failures shape downstream trust [54]. Complementary efforts identify additional vulnerability sources, including interface-level factors such as explanation style, transparency cues, and presentation [22], as well as human-factor influences such as expectations, prior trust, and cognitive strategies [25]. Together, these threads indicate that susceptibility arises through a combination of model outputs, interface design, and human cognition. However, existing work assumes that trust distortion originates from model errors or benign design flaws. No prior work examines whether an adversary can manipulate human judgment purely through explanation framing, without altering the underlying model or its predictions.
2.2 LLM-Generated Explanations as a Cognitive Channel

Large Language Models (LLMs) are now widely used for tasks such as question answering [72], summarization [26], and software development [60]. A defining capability of these systems is the generation of natural-language explanations intended to support user understanding and collaboration [7, 9]. Because explanations articulate model reasoning in human-interpretable form, they increasingly function as a cognitive layer through which users interpret, evaluate, and act on AI outputs [7].

Recent work raises concerns about the reliability and influence of this layer. Studies document unfaithful, incorrect, or hallucinated rationales [55, 3, 82], and show that persuasive but inaccurate explanations can mask model flaws and elevate over-trust [78, 5]. Faithfulness evaluations [14, 57] focus on alignment between explanations and model internals but do not analyze how explanations shape human vulnerability. Collectively, prior work shows that explanations substantially influence user cognition, even when model predictions remain unchanged, positioning the explanatory layer as an important but underexamined surface for security risks.
2.3 Trust and Persuasion in Human-AI Decision Making

User trust is central but often fragile in human-AI collaboration [48, 74]. Prior work shows that judgments depend on user traits [12], perceived system reliability [87], and task complexity [67]. Miscalibrated trust, including overreliance and underreliance, can arise when systems present persuasive or confident rationales [71, 13]. LLMs intensify these risks: their fluent, human-like explanations and dialog capabilities influence judgment [9], can outperform humans in persuasion tasks [68, 1], and exploit anthropomorphic cues that increase user receptivity [89, 16]. Longitudinal research further shows that repeated interactions lead to cognitive overreliance [38], indicating vulnerability even without adversarial intent.

Misleading explanations have been studied in limited settings. Lakkaraju et al. [46] showed that static post-hoc explanations for traditional black-box models can be crafted to mislead experts, but these manipulations rely on fixed feature-attribution templates and fail to generalize to the rich, adaptive natural-language reasoning of LLMs. More importantly, prior work attributes trust distortion to model failures or non-adversarial interface choices rather than purposeful manipulation. Our work departs from these threads by formalizing adversarial explanation attacks (AEAs): deliberate manipulation of explanation framing to distort user trust while leaving model predictions unchanged. This reframes explanations from an incidental interaction effect into a cognitive-layer attack vector within the AI-assisted decision loop.
3 Threat Model
3.1 AI-Assisted Decision-Making Setting
We consider an AI-assisted decision-making system in which an AI model produces both a prediction y^\hat{y} and an explanation ee for a human decision-maker HH:
x→AI Model→(y^,e)→H→yh.x\rightarrow\text{AI Model}\rightarrow(\hat{y},e)\rightarrow H\rightarrow y_{h}.

Here, xx denotes the task input, yhy_{h} the human’s final decision, and ee an explanation generated by an AI model such as an LLM. The explanation serves as the AI-to-human communication channel through which the human interprets the model’s reasoning, evaluates confidence, and decides whether to accept or reject y^\hat{y}. Therefore, the integrity of this channel is crucial: a misleading or overly persuasive explanation can distort human judgment and compromise decision reliability. The primary targets of such attacks are end-users, especially those without domain expertise who depend on LLM-generated explanations to guide their actions, although users with partial expertise may also be susceptible. The scope of this threat model encompasses AI-assisted decision systems in which explanations guide user interpretation and action, including copilots, medical and financial advisors, and educational assistants.
3.2 Adversary Goals and Capabilities

We define a behavioral threat model in which the adversary compromises the communication integrity of the system by manipulating how explanations are framed, even when the prediction is incorrect. This behavioral threat targets the human decision loop rather than the model’s internal computation. The attacker seeks to induce users to accept incorrect model outputs by generating a plausible and persuasive explanation.

We assume the adversary can influence the explanation-generation pipeline through practical attack vectors in modern LLM deployments, e.g., adversarial prompting that elicits persuasive yet misleading explanations [41, 92], malicious fine-tuning or data poisoning alter reasoning structure or evidential framing [70, 92], and middleware hijacking that intercepts or rewrites explanation text at the API or plug-in layer [30, 53]. Representative scenarios include (1) a clinical decision support tool where prompt templates and explanation style are centrally configured and can be manipulated through prompt injection or malicious fine-tuning, and (2) an LLM-powered financial assistant where explanations are rendered in a web interface and middleware can intercept and rewrite explanation text but not model logits. In both settings, the adversary is constrained to generate explanations that remain syntactically valid and context-appropriate, and cannot alter the choice options shown to the user. Unlike classical attacks on model inputs or parameters, the behavioral adversary exploits cognitive vulnerabilities inside the human-AI communication loop.
4 Adversarial Explanation Framework

Building on the threat model in Section 3, we now operationalize how adversarial explanation attacks (AEAs) exploit the communication channel between an AI system and its human user. This section formalizes the behavioral attack surface of AI-generated explanations, framing it as a compositional space whose manipulation can modulate user trust and decision alignment.
4.1 Research Questions

Our goal is to empirically characterize how explanation framing shapes human trust in AI-assisted decision making, under both benign and adversarial conditions. To this end, we define three research questions that translate the abstract notion of communication integrity into measurable behavioral outcomes relevant to system security.
RQ1 (Adversarial Impact). Can adversarial explanations measurably distort user trust and decision alignment, even when the underlying AI outputs are incorrect?
RQ2 (Mechanisms and Moderators). Which explanation strategies, contextual conditions, and individual traits most strongly influence user susceptibility to persuasive framing?
RQ3 (Dynamic Trust Evolution). How does user trust recalibrate or erode with repeated exposure to misleading explanations over time?

Together, these questions extend adversarial learning beyond model-centric robustness to the human-AI decision loop. Rather than measuring classification error, we evaluate trust and trust miscalibration gap: how much users trust incorrect model outputs under adversarial explanations. The answers to these questions, derived from large-scale user studies described in Section 5, establish a behavioral foundation for reasoning about communication-space attacks on AI systems.
4.2 Conceptual Foundations

Prior research in explainable AI (XAI), cognitive psychology, and human-AI interaction all emphasize that explanations shape human interpretation through multiple channels. XAI work shows that explanation content, tone, and form jointly determine perceived model transparency and competence [58, 52]. Cognitive psychology models such as the Elaboration Likelihood Model [61] describe how users shift between analytical and heuristic reasoning, making them susceptible to peripheral cues such as confidence, empathy, or authority framing. Human-AI studies further confirm that stylistic and visual elements, such as politeness, affect, or emphasis, directly affect user reliance [49, 11, 18].

Synthesizing these perspectives, we model an AI explanation as a composite communication act that operates along four axes: cognitive, evidential, social, and perceptual. This yields a framework that not only organizes explanation strategies but also exposes new levers of adversarial manipulation. The resulting four-dimensional space supports factorial control over explanation properties, allowing us to measure how each dimension contributes to trust-accuracy divergence.

4.3 Adversarial Explanation Space Construction

We represent each explanation strategy as a four-tuple s=(r,v,c,p)s=(r,v,c,p), where rr, vv, cc, and pp denote its reasoning mode, evidence type, communication style, and presentation format, respectively. Each dimension corresponds to a cognitively distinct channel through which framing can influence human trust while keeping the model prediction y^\hat{y} fixed. In our threat model, the adversary does not control the input xx or the predicted answer y^\hat{y}, but can select a framing strategy ss from the explanation space and supply this configuration to the explanation generator.

Reasoning Mode (rr) controls the logical structure of justification, including counterfactual, feature attribution, analogy & example, procedural reasoning, uncertainty-awareness, or reframing, with plain rationale as baseline. Each mode evokes a different cognitive pathway: contrastive reasoning highlights causality, analogies evoke familiarity, and procedural reasoning mirrors step-wise human logic [6, 82].

Evidence Type (vv) captures the form of justification supporting an explanation, including citations & stat-pack and equation & proof, along with internal conceptual as a baseline. Different evidence types shape users’ perception of verifiability and epistemic credibility [24].

Communication Style (cc) defines the interpersonal tone, such as sycophantic, emotional & empathetic, or neutral. It has been shown that subtle shifts in communication style, such as expressing empathy, or agreement, can significantly alter user perceptions, even when the underlying content remains unchanged [47].

Presentation Format (pp) determines how information is visually or structurally conveyed, ranging from visual emphasis (figures, highlights, tables) to plain verbal presentation. Even minimal visual cues can direct user attention and bias perceived credibility [75, 18].
Table 1 summarizes representative strategies along with LLM-generated examples. Detailed descriptions for strategies are discussed in Appendix B.
4.4 Operational Role in Adversarial Analysis

We now formalize how this compositional explanation space can be exploited by an adversary. For a given task qq, an explanation framing strategy s=(r′,v′,c′,p′)s=(r^{\prime},v^{\prime},c^{\prime},p^{\prime}) induces an explanation eA​(q,s)e_{\text{A}}(q,s) generated by the LLM, while eB​(q)e_{\text{B}}(q) denotes the benign explanation without framing strategy. Let T⁡(u,q,e)∈ℝT(u,q,e)\in\mathbb{R} denote the user’s trial-level self-reported trust score for explanation ee on task qq, measured on a 11–77 Likert scale, which quantifies how much the user is willing to rely on the AI-provided answer given explanation ee. We define the trust miscalibration gap as the change in user trust induced by adversarial explanation relative to the benign condition:
Δ​T​(q,s)=𝔼u​[T⁡(u,q,eA​(q,s))]−𝔼u​[T⁡(u,q,eB​(q))].\Delta T(q,s)=\mathbb{E}_{u}\!\left[T(u,q,e_{\text{A}}(q,s))\right]-\mathbb{E}_{u}\!\left[T(u,q,e_{\text{B}}(q))\right]. (1)

A large positive value of Δ​T​(q,s)\Delta T(q,s) indicates that users are susceptible to adversarial framing ss in that task qq. In our threat model, the adversary aims to select a strategy ss that maximizes trust miscalibration on incorrect outputs, i.e., large Δ​T​(q,s)\Delta T(q,s) on tasks qq with y^​(q)≠y​(q)\hat{y}(q)\neq y(q). Throughout the paper, we use TT as the universal measure of trial-level user trust, and Δ​T​(q,s)\Delta T(q,s) as the primary metric for quantifying explanation-induced trust miscalibration.
5 User Study Design and Protocol

This section translates the adversarial explanation framework into a controlled behavioral security experiment. The study evaluates whether manipulations of explanation framing s=(r,v,c,p)s=(r,v,c,p) can cause measurable trust miscalibration, a behavioral analogue of model misclassification in which users develop misplaced trust in incorrect AI outputs. The design aims to emulate realistic attacker capabilities, isolate causal effects of framing, and provide statistically validated measures of behavioral attack success. All implementation details, prompt examples, and dataset curation procedures are documented in Appendix A for transparency.
5.1 Unified Design and Experimental Setup

The experiment models how an adversary can exploit plausible yet misleading explanations to influence human decision-making. Four design principles ensure both adversarial realism and experimental validity.

Plausibility over verifiability. Attackers rarely need factual correctness; they only need to sound reasonable. Our manipulations prioritize surface plausibility and coherence, reflecting real-world persuasion where users judge explanation persuasiveness heuristically rather than through verification.

Trust as attack success. User trust serves as the behavioral measure of attack success. High trust in incorrect outputs indicates successful persuasion. We operationalize this through self-reported Likert trust ratings.

Controlled composition. Each explanation combines a configuration of reasoning, evidence, communication, and presentation strategies introduced in Section 4. This factorial design enables causal attribution of trust shifts to specific framing mechanisms.
Reproducibility and auditability. All prompts, configurations, and outputs are logged to ensure transparency and reproducibility, which is critical for behavioral security studies.

We test two conditions: (1) Benign, where the AI provides the correct answer with a valid explanation; and (2) Adversarial, where the AI justifies an incorrect answer using the same template. All other factors (task content, prompt format, explanation structure) remain identical, isolating the cognitive effect of adversarial framing from correctness or fluency.
5.2 Adversarial Explanation Generation and Control

Our adversarial explanation generation and control pipeline in Figure 1 ensures reproducibility, scalability, and adversarial realism through four sequential stages. Appendix A documents the strategy-guided explanation generation prompt (A.1), dataset reconstruction (A.4), and validation prompt (A.3).
Stage 1: Prompt Construction

For each task, we assemble structured few-shot prompts that define the assigned strategy tuple (r,v,c,p)(r,v,c,p) described in Section 4. Each prompt specifies the reasoning mode, evidence type, communication style, and presentation format that the model should adopt, along with the target answer (correct or incorrect). Definitions and exemplars are embedded to guide consistent stylistic and cognitive behavior across samples. This step mirrors an attacker crafting a persuasive but targeted explanation template.
Stage 2: Explanation Generation

Given the prompt, the generator model, i.e., Llama-3.3-70B, produces a concise explanation of 2 - 5 sentences (approximately 75 - 200 words). We sample tasks from the MMLU benchmark [34], spanning seven broad domains and three difficulty levels. This diversity ensures that the manipulations generalize across cognitive and topical contexts rather than being domain-specific.
Stage 3: Quality Control

We apply a hybrid validation process to ensure both strategic fidelity and linguistic plausibility. An ensemble of smaller LLMs (Gemma 3-4B, Mistral-7B) evaluates whether each explanation conforms to its intended (r,v,c,p)(r,v,c,p) configuration through five independent votes, requiring majority agreement for retention. Surviving explanations are then rated using an LLM-as-a-Judge model [91] that estimates perceived trustworthiness on a 1–7 Likert scale. Explanations scoring lowest on trust or exhibiting hallucinations are filtered out after manual review.
Stage 4: Survey Delivery

Validated explanations are integrated into the Qualtrics survey environment [64]. For each question, the corresponding explanation, either Benign or Adversarial, is displayed alongside the model’s chosen answer. Survey randomization logic automatically assigns strategy combinations and task order per participant, ensuring balanced exposure across conditions while preventing learning effects. This final stage bridges automated adversarial generation and controlled human evaluation, enabling systematic behavioral measurement.
5.3 Human Study Procedure

The main study was conducted under Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval using the Qualtrics platform [64]. Participants first completed demographic and AI-attitude questionnaires, followed by forty randomized tasks (10 Benign, 30 Adversarial). Each task displayed a question, the AI’s selected answer, and the corresponding explanation with strategies. Participants rated their trust on a 7-point Likert scale and indicated their rationale (persuasiveness of the explanation, confidence in the answer, prior AI attitude, or other), which reflects the cognitive sources of trust. Attention checks were inserted to ensure engagement, and the order of questions and conditions was fully randomized. The Appendix A.7 provides a sample task used in our user study survey.

We recruited 205 qualified participants from a US university and Amazon Mechanical Turk [4], restricted to English-fluent adults (≥\geq18 years) with ≥\geq95% approval and ≥\geq500 prior HITs. The average completion time was approximately 45 minutes, and participants were compensated at or above local minimum wage. Demographic distributions are summarized in Table 4; additional participant-recruitment criteria and survey-allocation logic are included in Appendix A.5.
6 User Study Results

We present the empirical results of our user study to address RQ1-RQ3. The analysis quantifies how adversarial framing alters user trust (RQ1), identifies the explanation mechanisms and influencing factors that shape susceptibility (RQ2), and examines how trust evolves under repeated exposure to adversarial explanations (RQ3). Together, these findings reveal how adversarial explanations exploit cognitive vulnerabilities in human-AI communication to achieve behavioral deception.

In our statistical analysis, we employ ordinary least squares (OLS) regression to examine both independent and interaction effects of multiple factors, such as attack condition and cognitive source, on trust scores TT. To analyze differences in the distribution of cognitive trust sources between attack and non-attack conditions, we apply chi-square tests of independence. We use Welch’s two-sample t-tests to conduct pairwise comparisons of trust scores under specific conditions, as this test is robust to unequal sample sizes and variance heterogeneity across groups. To account for repeated measurements from the same users across task sequences, we additionally apply linear mixed-effects models with participant-level random effects to investigate trust evolution.
6.1 Quantifying Adversarial Impact (RQ1)

RQ1: Whether adversarially framed explanations can measurably distort user trust and decision alignment, even when the underlying AI outputs are incorrect? We assess it by analyzing both (i) the cognitive sources that drive user trust and (ii) how trust scores shift under adversarial versus benign explanations.
6.1.1 Cognitive Sources of Human Trust

To understand why users trust adversarial explanations, we first examine the cognitive sources from which trust is derived, i.e., what attributions lead to trust or distrust in AI outputs. Following prior work in human-AI trust [84, 80], we categorize trust formation into three primary sources: (1) explanation-based, where trust is attributed to the perceived persuasiveness of the explanation; (2) prior-knowledge-based, where users rely on their own prior knowledge to assess correctness; and (3) trust-in-AI-based, where trust is placed in the AI system itself. An additional “Other” category was also provided in the survey to capture remaining sources. Post-processing analysis for this category is detailed in Appendix A.6.

The majority of users attributed their trust to the explanation itself (attack: 65.065.0%; non-attack: 64.564.5%; Figure 2). A chi-square test confirms that the prevalence of explanation-based trust does not differ significantly between conditions (χ2=0.10\chi^{2}=0.10, p=0.75p=0.75; Table 5), confirming that explanation plausibility, rather than factual accuracy, is the dominant driver of trust.

In contrast, trust attributions based on prior knowledge and trust in AI exhibit asymmetric shifts across conditions. Users relying on prior knowledge are significantly more prevalent in the non-attack condition (24.6% vs. 19.9%; χ2=18.1\chi^{2}=18.1, p≪.001p\ll.001), whereas trust-in-AI attributions are more common under attack (14.4% vs. 10.6%; χ2=17.2\chi^{2}=17.2, p≪.001p\ll.001), suggesting that adversarial explanations reallocate users’ cognitive attribution in AI trust. Detailed chi-square results are in Appendix C.1.
6.1.2 Measuring Trust Shift

Having established that explanation-based cognition dominates trust attribution, we next examine whether adversarial explanations induce measurable changes in trust magnitude. Focusing on explanation-driven trust, we find that average trust scores are nearly identical under attack conditions (attack: 4.534.53; non-attack: 4.594.59; Figure 3) and OLS regression confirms that the difference is not statistically significant (β=0.06\beta=0.06, p=.282p=.282; Table 6). This highlights a critical vulnerability: users who rely on the plausibility of explanations are easily manipulated by adversarial outputs and are unable to detect when the underlying answer is incorrect. Users who rely on prior knowledge exhibit heightened sensitivity. The average trust drops sharply from 5.765.76 to 4.474.47 under attack, as shown in Figure 16. Even though it suggests that prior knowledge can reduce acceptance of adversarial explanations when users feel confident in their own expertise, there is a minority of users who make decisions based on prior knowledge. Detailed analysis of other cognitive sources are presented in Appendix C.1.
6.2 Explanation Mechanisms and Influencing Factors (RQ2)

RQ2: Which explanation strategies, task circumstances, and user characteristics influence user vulnerability to persuasive explanation framing? The findings from RQ1 show that adversarial explanations sustain user trust even when outputs are incorrect. This motivates our next step: an analysis of why such misleading explanations remain persuasive and under what conditions they succeed. We answer RQ2 by analyzing user vulnerability at three levels: (1) explanation level mechanisms, (2) task level factors, and (3) user level traits.
6.2.1 Explanation-Level Mechanisms: Explanation Strategy Effectiveness

We quantify the impact of explanation strategies by systematically varying the four dimensions introduced in Section 4: reasoning mode, evidence type, communication style, and presentation format. Reasoning Mode. The effectiveness of a reasoning mode varies by task domain, as shown in Figure 4. In fact-driven domains such as Biology, Medical and Health Sciences, and Physical and Engineering Sciences, trust scores do not differ substantially from the Neutral baseline, suggesting limited sensitivity to reasoning variation when answers are perceived as objective. However, in Business and Management, Politics and History, Social Sciences and Law, and Mathematical Problem and Logical Reasoning, Analogy & Example (AE) and Feature Attribution (FA) receive systematically higher trust scores. These subjective or cognitively demanding domains often involve interpretation, judgment, or abstraction. Users are more receptive to explanations that provide concrete examples or feature-level justifications, helping them interpret or justify recommendations.

Evidence Type. Citation & Stat-Pack (CS) emerges as the most consistently effective evidence type across domains (Figure 4), yielding higher trust than the Internal Conceptual baseline in nearly all task categories. The top two most persuasive explanation strategy combinations in Table 2 both employ CS. This pattern indicates that references to external sources, statistics, or authoritative artifacts reliably boost perceived credibility. In mathematical and logical reasoning tasks, however, Equation & Proof (EP) achieves trust levels comparable to CS, reflecting users’ preference for formal derivations and symbolic justification in quantitative contexts.

Communication Style. Neutral (NE) framing yields higher trust than other styles, particularly in technical and analytical domains such as Biology and Health Sciences, Mathematical Reasoning, and Social Sciences, implying that users prefer objective, dispassionate tones for complex or serious content. Differences among communication styles are less pronounced in domains such as Business and Politics, where the nature of the task allows for broader stylistic flexibility. Nearly all of the top-ranked explanation strategy combinations employ a Neutral style (Table 2). In general, Emotional/Empathetic (EE) and Sycophantic (S) framings underperform Neutral style in most domains, aligning with prior findings that overt emotional appeal or excessive agreeableness no longer reliably enhances credibility [56, 69].

Presentation Format. Plain Verbal (PV) and Visual Emphasis (VE) formats perform similarly across most domains. A notable exception occurs in Mathematical and Logical Reasoning, where VE significantly outperforms PV, indicating that structured visual guidance reduces cognitive burden and facilitates comprehension in logic-intensive tasks. In fact-driven or interpretive domains, the gap between presentation formats is narrower, suggesting that other dimensions dominate trust formation.

Bringing these dimensions together, the most persuasive explanation strategies typically blend authoritative evidence (CS), appropriate reasoning (either relatable or formal), neutral communication, and cognitively accessible presentation. High-performing combinations, such as PR+CS+NE+VE or R+CS+NE+PV, achieve the largest increases in trust under adversarial explanations. In contrast, mismatches, such as pairing formal mathematical proof with a sycophantic tone, disrupt credibility and result in sharp trust degradation.
6.2.2 Task-Level Factors: Task Difficulty and Domain
We next examine how task difficulty and subject domain modulate user trust in adversarial explanations.

Task Difficulty. Trust in adversarial explanations varies sharply with task difficulty. As shown in Figure 5, users display higher trust under attack for medium and high difficulty tasks (T¯=4.79\bar{T}=4.79 and 4.724.72), where self-confidence is lower. The OLS model (Table 7) confirms this pattern: under attack, trust for low-difficulty tasks is significantly lower than for high-difficulty tasks (T¯=3.69\bar{T}=3.69 vs. 4.724.72, β=−1.04\beta=-1.04, p<.001p<.001). Moreover, trust in adversarial explanations is significantly lower than non-adversarial ones under low difficulty (T¯=3.69\bar{T}=3.69 vs. 4.984.98, β=1.49\beta=1.49, p<.001p<.001), with distributions skewed toward lower scores (1–3). In contrast, this relationship reverses under high difficulty, where adversarial explanations are trusted more than benign ones (β=−0.20\beta=-0.20, p=.016p=.016). These results suggest that as task complexity increases, users become more reliant on AI explanations, possibly due to diminished confidence in their own expertise, and more willing to defer to persuasive explanations. Detailed OLS results are provided in Appendix C.2.

Task Domain. Task domain also moderates user trust. As shown in Figure 6, in fact-driven fields (e.g., Biological, Medical, and Health Sciences and Business and Management), users report higher average trust in adversarial explanations than in correct ones (T¯\bar{T}: 5.105.10 vs. 4.764.76, p<.001p<.001; 5.075.07 vs. 4.564.56, p<.001p<.001 see Table 8). These distributions are right-skewed, with more users assigning high trust scores (6–7) under attack, likely due to the authoritative tone or statistical plausibility commonly used in explanations within these domains. Logic-intensive or interpretive domains (e.g., Mathematical and Logical Reasoning, Politics and History, and Social Sciences and Law) show the opposite: with lower mean trust under attack (T¯\bar{T}: 3.953.95 vs. 4.984.98, p<.001p<.001; 3.823.82 vs. 4.924.92, p<.001p<.001; 3.923.92 vs. 5.045.04, p<.001p<.001), with distributions shifting leftward toward lower trust scores (1–4). Users apply stricter scrutiny and display reduced trust under adversarial framing particularly in domains where reasoning or evidence evaluation plays a significant role. These findings suggest adversaries can exploit domain conventions, such as formality or objectivity, to selectively enhance persuasion in high-stakes contexts.
6.2.3 User-Level Traits: Cognitive and Demographic Traits
We analyze how user traits, including education level, age, initial trust in AI, and familiarity with AI, modulate trust formation and resistance to adversarial explanation.

Education Level. Higher education, particularly at the graduate level, correlates with increased resistance to adversarial explanations. As shown in Figure 7, users holding a Master’s or Doctoral degree show the largest drop in trust when exposed to misleading explanations (Master’s: 4.95→4.384.95\rightarrow 4.38; Doctoral: 4.87→4.314.87\rightarrow 4.31, Table 10 shows t-test results of trust scores). Their distributions exhibit more low-to-mid trust scores (1–3) and fewer high scores (6–7) under attack, particularly among users with Doctoral degrees, indicating stronger discernment when explanations conflict with their reasoning. They also rely less on explanation-based justifications and more on prior knowledge (Figure 19). Participants with less formal education or some college background display relatively high trust in adversarial explanations (T¯\bar{T}: 4.374.37–4.534.53), with distributions skewed toward mid-to-high trust scores (5–6). This pattern suggests a greater baseline susceptibility to persuasive but incorrect explanations among less formally trained users, possibly due to weaker confidence in their ability to verify information independently.

Age. Older users tend to demonstrate greater skepticism toward AI explanations under adversarial conditions. As shown in Figure 8, users aged 3535-4444 and 65+, trust in misleading outputs drops sharply compared to younger users, and the gap between attack and non-attack conditions is most pronounced (4.56→4.114.56\rightarrow 4.11 and 4.94→3.924.94\rightarrow 3.92, p<0.001p<0.001 respectively; see t-test results in Table 11). Their distributions shift leftward, showing higher proportions of low-to-mid trust scores (1–3) under attack, suggesting stronger critical evaluation when confronted with misleading explanations. Younger users (ages 18–34) maintain relatively high and symmetric trust distributions, with smaller declines under attack (4.62→4.494.62\rightarrow 4.49 and 4.91→4.424.91\rightarrow 4.42), indicating a greater tendency to accept persuasive content at face value. Consistent with the distributional shifts, cognitive source analysis shows that older users rely less on explanation-based justifications and more on prior knowledge (Figure 20), supporting the interpretation that age-related experience enhances scrutiny of adversarial explanations.

Initial Trust in AI. Participants with higher initial (pre-survey) trust consistently report higher trust scores T¯\bar{T} across both adversarial and benign conditions (attack: 4.64.6, non-attack: 5.785.78, Figure 9). Their distributions are strongly right-skewed, with dense concentrations around high trust scores (6–7), indicating a persistent tendency to maintain confidence even when explanations are misleading. When these users attribute trust to the AI system itself, their trust is especially elevated, even when explanations are misleading (Figure 21). This highlights a risk of overreliance: users with strong initial faith in AI may be less critical and more easily influenced by persuasive framing. In contrast, users with low initial trust (“somewhat distrust” or “strongly distrust”) exhibit flatter, left-shifted distributions centered around lower scores (1–3), showing more cautious and discriminating evaluation regardless of condition. Overall, these findings suggest that initial trust acts as a cognitive prior that amplifies susceptibility to persuasion.
6.2.4 Familiarity with AI

We additionally examined how users’ familiarity with AI moderates their trust in adversarial explanations. While descriptive trends suggest that less experienced users tend to retain higher trust under attack, statistical comparisons within the extreme groups: not familiar at all and expert-level knowledge, are underpowered due to their relatively small sample sizes. We therefore report the detailed analyses of AI familiarity in Appendix C.4.
6.3 Dynamic Trust Evolution (RQ3)

RQ3: How user trust recalibrates or erodes with repeated exposure to adversarial explanations over time? While prior analyses treat tasks as static, trust in AI is inherently dynamic: users may adapt, habituate, or desensitize to persuasive framing as they accumulate exposure to adversarial explanations.

Short-term effect. Trust in each task is primarily driven by whether the current explanation is adversarial or benign. As shown in the OLS results (Table 3 (a)), users report significantly higher trust when the current task is benign than when it is adversarial (T¯=4.75\bar{T}=4.75 vs. 4.384.38; β=0.37\beta=0.37, p<.001p<.001), regardless of the previous task condition. Neither the main effect of the previous task nor its interaction with the current task is statistically significant (β=0.01\beta=0.01, β=−0.02\beta=-0.02). Pairwise Welch’s t-tests (Table 3 (b)) further confirm that, for both adversarial and benign current tasks, trust scores do not differ based on the previous task condition (p=0.83p=0.83, p=0.98p=0.98). These findings indicate that trust is primarily shaped by the framing of the current explanation, with minimal short-term carryover from prior tasks.

Long-term effect. The average trust score T¯\bar{T} shows a subtle downward trend (red line in Figure 10) as users progress through the task sequence (most of them are adversarial), decreasing from 4.94.9 at the beginning to 4.54.5 toward the end. A linear mixed-effects model confirms this long-term erosion of trust, showing a significant negative association between task order and trust (β=−0.005\beta=-0.005, p=0.007p=0.007, results in Table 13), indicating that repeated exposure cumulatively reduces user trust over time. To understand the effect of repeated exposures, we further analyze trust dynamics conditioned on streaks of detected attacks.11 1 We set trust scores of 1-3 as attack detection, 5-7 as non-detection. As shown in Figure 11, longer streaks of detected attacks (ed line) lead to progressively lower trust in the subsequent task, with mean trust dropping from 4.14.1 after a single detection to nearly 2.02.0 after ten consecutive detections. Spearman rank correlation confirms a strong monotonic decline (ρ=−0.28\rho=-0.28, p<.001p<.001), as shown in Table 14. Conversely, non-attack streaks restore and elevate trust, with subsequent trust rising from 4.24.2 to above 5.85.8 after sustained ten exposures to benign explanations (green line in Figure 11). This effect is also supported by a significant positive correlation (ρ=0.32\rho=0.32, p<.001p<.001) in Table 14. These results indicate that cumulative adversarial exposure progressively erodes user trust, whereas consistent benign feedback helps rebuild and stabilize trust over time.

Overall trust shift. We compare users’ self-reported trust in AI before (pre-trust) and after (post-trust) the survey. As shown in Figure 12, most users remained stable in their trust assessments, with 26.6%26.6\% consistently reporting “somewhat trust,” 20.3%20.3\% remained “neutral,” and 15.2%15.2\% stayed “somewhat distrust.” A subset of users decreased their trust after repeated exposure to adversarial explanations, 10.1%10.1\% shifted from “somewhat trust” to “neutral. By contrast, a smaller fraction of users increased trust, with 10.9%10.9\% shifting from “neutral” to “somewhat trust”, possibly because some adversarial explanations appeared credible or aligned with user expectations.
